chapter.title: Know who's walking with you

cards.body: You'd never stop a friend on their own street to point out their own front door. On a walk you only point at what the people beside you can't already see, and **what they already know decides what you leave out**. Most speakers skip this step and point at everything.
cards.simpler: Think of walking with a friend down their own street. You wouldn't stop and point at their front door. They see it every day. On a walk, you only point at things the people beside you can't already see. **What they already know decides what you leave out.** Most speakers skip this step. They point at everything, even the things everyone can see.

cards.prompt: Priya has 3 minutes to tell her five-a-side football team about the new training schedule. Which part should she cut?

options.text: A quick explanation of what five-a-side football is
The date the new schedule starts

whyNot.b: That's the thing they don't know yet and care about most: it stays.
whyNot.c: That's new information they'll act on: a date is the last thing to cut.

cards.reteach: Her team plays five-a-side every week. Telling them what it is spends 20 of her 180 seconds and shows she hasn't thought about who's listening. Cut what they already know. Keep what's new and what they'll act on.

cards.title: Three lines about them
cards.body:
Before you plan a single step of the route, write *three lines* about the people walking with you. Line 1: who they are, in one phrase. Line 2: what they already know about your subject. Line 3: what they want to leave with.

Those three lines are a **filter, not a form**. Hold each part of your talk up against line 2. If they already know it, it goes. Hold the rest against line 3. If they don't want it, it goes too.

You'd think the lines would be extra work. They save work: most of a first draft explains things to people who were already there.
cards.simpler: Before you plan your talk, write three lines about your listeners. Who they are. What they already know about your subject. What they want to take away. **The lines are a filter, not a form.** Hold each part of your talk against line two. If they already know it, drop it. Hold the rest against line three. If they don't want it, drop it too. They save work. Most first drafts explain things to people who already knew them.

cards.title: Tomás and the bike racks
cards.body: Tomás had 3 minutes at his building's residents' meeting to argue for bike racks in the courtyard. His first draft spent 40 seconds on when the building went up and how the courtyard was laid out. Then he wrote his three lines: *neighbours who've lived here 5 years or more; they know the courtyard, the bins and the broken gate; they want to know what it costs them*. The history went. The talk shrank to 2 and a half minutes, and the first question from the floor was about cost, which he'd already answered in his second sentence.
cards.simpler: Tomás had three minutes at his residents' meeting to ask for bike racks. His first draft spent forty seconds on the building's history and layout. Then he wrote his three lines: neighbours of five years or more, who knew the courtyard, the bins and the broken gate, and wanted to know the cost. **The history went.** The talk shrank to two and a half minutes. The first question was about cost. He had answered it in sentence two.

cards.prompt: Jo is speaking to parents at her son's school about a new pickup gate. Which three lines will actually help her cut?

options.text: Parents at the school. Busy people. Mostly nice.
Parents who do the 3.15 pickup. They know the queue down the road. They want to know if the new gate means less waiting.
About 20 people. Tuesday evening. The school hall.

whyNot.a: Those are adjectives, not what they know or want: 'busy' doesn't tell you one thing to cut.
whyNot.c: That's the room, not the people's heads: a headcount and a time change nothing in your talk.

cards.reteach: The three lines only work when line 2 and line 3 are specific. 'They know the queue' tells Jo to skip describing the problem. 'They want less waiting' tells her to lead with the answer. Adjectives and headcounts can't do either.

cards.title: Cut, then lead with what they want
cards.body:
Here's the reversal. You'd think learning more about your listeners means adding more for them. It's the opposite: **every line you learn about them is a line you get to cut**. Knowing they've all rattled the broken gate means you never describe it.

Line 3 does one more job. Whatever they want to leave with goes near the front, not saved for a big finish. Tomás put the cost in sentence two because that's where their attention already was.

If you don't know them, ask the organiser one question: 'what do these people already know about this?' A single reply beats guessing.
cards.simpler: More about your listeners does not mean more in the talk. **Every line you learn about them is a line you get to cut.** If they have all rattled the broken gate, you never describe it. Line three has one more job. Put what they want near the start, not at the end. Tomás put the cost in sentence two, where their attention was. Don't know them? Ask the organiser what they already know. One answer beats guessing.

cards.body: Lena gave a 3-minute update to the six people she'd worked beside for 2 years, and spent the first minute explaining what their team does. Phones came out at 0:40. The tell is easy to spot: **if the person in the front row could have said the sentence themselves, it isn't a sentence, it's a delay**. Read your draft and ask that of every line.
cards.simpler: Lena gave a three-minute update to six people she had worked beside for two years. She spent the first minute explaining what their team does. Phones came out at forty seconds. Here is the easy test. **If the person in the front row could have said the sentence themselves, it isn't a sentence, it's a delay.** Read your draft and ask that of every line.

cards.prompt: Sam's talk runs 3 minutes 30 and needs to lose 30 seconds. Where does he look first?

options.text: The parts his listeners already know
The one point the talk exists to make

whyNot.b: That's the arrival: losing it is how talks trail off, not how they get shorter.
whyNot.c: That's the destination from chapter 1: cut it and there's no walk left, just 3 minutes of wandering.

cards.reteach: The first cut is always what the audience already knows, because it costs them nothing to lose. Your one sentence and your close are the start and end of the route. Everything they could have told you themselves is the padding.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body:
Write 3 lines about your listeners: who they are, what they already know, what they want to leave with. Then **cut everything they already know** and move what they want toward the front.

Tomorrow: why three things stick from a good talk and nothing from a bad one.
cards.simpler: Write three lines about your listeners. Who they are. What they already know. What they want to leave with. Then **cut everything they already know**, and move what they want toward the front of the talk. Tomorrow we look at why three things stick from a good talk and nothing sticks from a bad one.

cards.body: Open your notes app. Write 3 lines about the people who'll hear your talk: who they are, what they already know, what they want. Then cross out one thing from your talk they already know.
cards.simpler: Open your notes app. Write three lines about the people who will hear your talk. Who they are. What they already know. What they want. Now look at your talk and find one thing they already know. **Cross it out.** That is one less thing to say.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now describe your listeners in 3 lines and cut any part of your talk they don't need.
